**The Stairway to a Forgotten Era**

    In the year 1350, the world took a different turn. The Black Death, which ravaged Europe in the 14th century, had a profound impact on the social and economic structures of the time. Instead of leading to the rise of a middle class and the decline of feudalism, the plague accelerated the feudal system's decline, allowing the nobility to consolidate their power and maintain their grip on society.

    As the centuries passed, the feudal system evolved, becoming more complex and rigid. The nobility continued to hold sway over the common folk, who were bound to the land and forced to provide labor, goods, and services to their lords in exchange for protection and the right to live on the land.

    The absence of a strong middle class meant that the economy was heavily dependent on the whims of the nobility, leading to a stagnant and inefficient system. Trade and commerce were limited, and the concept of money as we know it today did not exist. Instead, goods and services were bartered or exchanged for other goods and services.

    The lack of a strong central government meant that power was fragmented among the nobility, leading to a series of petty wars and conflicts over territory and influence. The nobility became increasingly isolated and withdrawn, living in fortified castles and manor houses, surrounded by their own private armies and retinues.

    As the centuries went by, the feudal system became more and more entrenched, with the nobility holding absolute power over the common folk. The concept of individual freedom and equality was all but forgotten, and the idea of a meritocratic society where individuals could rise to positions of power based on their talents and abilities was lost forever.

    In this world, the concept of a "middle class" never existed. The nobility were the only ones who held power and influence, and the common folk were relegated to a life of servitude and drudgery.

    The absence of a strong middle class also meant that the arts and sciences suffered. The nobility were more interested in maintaining their power and wealth than in pursuing knowledge and innovation. The universities and libraries that once flourished in Europe were reduced to mere relics of a bygone era, and the pursuit of scientific and artistic knowledge was all but forgotten.

    As the centuries went by, the feudal system became more and more rigid, with the nobility holding absolute power over the common folk. The idea of a "social contract" between the nobility and the common folk was lost forever, and the concept of individual rights and freedoms was all but forgotten.

    In this world, the concept of a "democracy" never existed. The nobility were the only ones who held power, and the common folk were relegated to a life of servitude and drudgery.

    The feudal system continued to dominate society for centuries, until it was eventually replaced by a new system of governance, one that was even more rigid and oppressive than the one that came before.

    And so, the world continued on its path, with the nobility holding absolute power over the common folk, and the concept of individual freedom and equality all but forgotten.
